'We've become dumb!' GOP at war with itself as Big Oil slams Trump's diesel plan
articles.description: A decades-long alliance between congressional Republicans and the fossil fuel industry is fracturing over a proposed diesel export ban , with farm-state GOP lawmakers and MAGA populists now openly attacking "Big Oil" as skyrocketing fuel prices threaten Republicans' standing heading into November. The White House is weighing a 90-day halt on diesel exports, an idea Trump himself has publicly floated as fuel prices climb toward record territory. Oil industry advocates warn the move would backfire, arguing it could actually worsen an already difficult fuel market rather than fix it. Rather than blame the Iran war and the administration's own foreign policy for driving up prices, many conservatives are instead directing their frustration squarely at the oil industry. Energy lobbyist Mike McKenna, who worked in Trump's first White House, worries the rift signals something bigger than a policy disagreement. "We've become literally as dumb as the other side," he said. That's a stark shift for a relationship that's historically been mutually beneficial: oil companies got favorable policy, and Republicans got dependable campaign cash. Just this year, virtually the whole GOP caucus lined up behind a major budget bill containing a laundry list of drilling-friendly provisions. Not every Republican strategist thinks the anger will stick. Arizona-based GOP consultant Barrett Marson predicted the current frustration is a temporary reaction that will fade once the Iran conflict winds down. The tension has spilled directly onto the Senate floor, where oil-state Republicans are clashing with farm-state colleagues pushing the export ban, led by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA). Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) voiced skepticism that restricting exports would meaningfully move prices given how globally interconnected fuel supply really is, while Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) argued the better fix is restarting idled refineries, including two shut down in California under strict state environmental rules. Diesel prices have climbed to roughly $6.52 a gallon nationally, nearly $3 higher than a year ago, squeezing farm states like Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska where Republicans now face competitive Senate races that weren't on anyone's radar a year earlier. Democrats have dismissed the export ban proposal as a political gimmick, arguing Republicans are avoiding the real fix: pressuring Trump to end the war in Iran that's driving the price spike in the first place.

articles.title: UK losing up to £6.5bn a year in EU trade due to mismatched product rules
articles.description: IPPR finds failure to align testing standards has forced companies to abandon exporting to EU and is costing costing 0.18% of national income The UK is losing out on annual exports to the EU that could be worth as much as £6.5bn without a deal with Brussels that allows manufacturers to jettison duplicate product testing. In the latest attempt to calculate the loss of trade with the EU after Brexit, the IPPR thinktank said many companies have given up selling goods to the EU or set up subsidiaries inside the trade bloc after successive governments failed to secure a mutual recognition agreement that would avoid the extra administration costs. Motor vehicle and part exports would have been between £2.48bn and £3.42bn higher each year. Electronic exports could have been between £1.17bn and £1.67bn higher. Pharmaceutical exports would have had an estimated annual uplift of between £740m and £820m. Continue reading...

New Trump comments 'blindsided' allies and led to flurry of panicked calls: report
articles.description: Oil executives thought they'd beaten back a diesel export ban. Then President Donald Trump opened his mouth at the United Nations — and sent the industry into a full-blown panic . On "the sidelines" of the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Trump said he's considering restricting diesel exports as prices hit record highs just weeks before the midterms, according to the Wall Street Journal. The comment "blindsided" oil executives, including some Trump donors, who believed they'd already won the fight to keep shipments flowing, and lobbyists reportedly scrambled to call White House officials and congressional Republicans to register their objections. It didn't matter — insiders now say some form of export limit looks "inevitable," the Journal reported. "I think we've invested too much in developing customers overseas, and this is the wrong signal," Dan Eberhart, CEO of oil-field services firm Canary and a Trump donor, told the Journal. According to the Journal report, "Even if the measure is temporary, U.S. oil companies stand to lose billions of dollars in revenue if they aren’t allowed to ship diesel abroad." Trump is giving every indication that he is siding with vulnerable Republicans over his own oil-industry allies: Iowa Republicans, including Sen. Chuck Grassley, have pushed hard for a ban , arguing "sky-high diesel costs" are crushing farmers. A White House official said Trump "wants to see gas prices at the pump fall and is evaluating all options on the table." One energy consultant with ties to refiners told the Journal, "It's all hands on deck. But it doesn't matter. We're not debating policy anymore. They've got to win a couple of key Senate races. The only way to do that is to put the export ban in temporarily." Industry officials warn the move could backfire by spurring "international prices for the fuel to skyrocket" and lead to "retaliation' from other countries — the kind of unintended consequences that have already drawn scorn from Wall Street Journal's own editorial board .
